In regulated or fast-moving domains it's often the difference between a usable system and one nobody trusts.
diagram2:
source changes
  ↓ detected? reparsed? re-embedded?
  ↓ upserted? searchable?
retrievable

Broken stage → no error at the user's end.
Retrieval keeps confidently serving last week.

Monitor END TO END, not job exit codes:
  write a canary doc, time until retrievable
  alert on lag, not on failure

Show "last updated" with retrieved content.
Silent staleness → visible caveat.

means: Training a base model on instruction-response pairs so it follows directions instead of merely continuing text. It's why chat models feel usable at all.
example: A raw base model given a question continues with more questions. The instruction-tuned version answers, because it was trained on the shape of the interaction.
diagram:
base model:        predicts the next token
instruction-tuned: follows an instruction
+ preference-tuned: prefers helpful, safe answers

You almost never want a raw base model in a product
how:
A base model is trained to predict the next token in text. That's all. Give one a question and it may well continue with more questions, because that's a plausible continuation of a document containing a question.

Instruction tuning is a second training phase on examples of instructions paired with good responses. It teaches the model that when text looks like a request, the appropriate continuation is a helpful answer.

This is what makes the technology usable as a product rather than a curiosity, and it's why every model you'd actually deploy has been through it.

A third phase usually follows — preference tuning, via RLHF or DPO — which shapes *which* helpful answer it prefers: more accurate, better formatted, less likely to produce something harmful.
more: Worth knowing because it explains a real behaviour: instruction-tuned models are biased toward being helpful, which contributes to hallucination. Asked something it doesn't know, a model shaped to answer will produce an answer. Abstention has to be built deliberately — through prompting, grounding and an explicit escalation path — because the training pushed the other way.
diagram2:
base model
  "What is the capital of France?"
  → "What is the capital of Spain? What is..."
     (a plausible continuation of a document)

+ instruction tuning
  → "Paris."

+ preference tuning (RLHF / DPO)
  → accurate, well-formatted, safer

Side effect worth knowing:
  trained to be helpful → answers even when
  it shouldn't → abstention must be built in.

means: How often independent human labellers agree. Low agreement means your task definition is ambiguous, and no model can beat an ambiguous target.
example: Two annotators agreed on only 62% of 'is this response helpful' labels. The guidelines were rewritten with examples before any model work continued.
diagram:
2+ annotators label the same items
  ↓ measure agreement (Cohen's kappa)
  <0.6  → your task definition is broken
  >0.8  → a usable ceiling for the model

Model accuracy cannot exceed label quality
how:
Before trusting any labelled dataset, check whether two people labelling the same items agree.

If they don't, the task is ambiguous — and that has a hard consequence: no model can exceed the consistency of its labels. Training or evaluating against data humans disagree about means measuring noise and calling it accuracy.

Cohen's kappa is the usual measure, and it corrects for agreement that would happen by chance. Below about 0.6 the guidelines need rewriting. Above 0.8 you have a usable ceiling.

The most valuable output isn't the number, it's the disagreements themselves. Reading the cases two annotators labelled differently shows you exactly where the definition is unclear — and that's usually where your model is failing too, for the same reason.
more: Run this before labelling at scale, not after. Discovering low agreement once ten thousand items are labelled means either relabelling or accepting a dataset you know is unreliable. A hundred double-labelled items up front costs almost nothing and regularly saves the whole exercise.
diagram2:
2 annotators label the same 100 items
  ↓ Cohen's kappa (chance-corrected)

  < 0.6  → the task definition is broken
  0.6-0.8 → usable, tighten the guidelines
  > 0.8  → a solid ceiling for the model

Model accuracy CANNOT exceed label quality.

The disagreements are the real output:
  they show exactly where the definition is unclear
  — which is where the model fails too.

Do this BEFORE labelling 10,000 items.

means: Training a small model to imitate a large one's outputs. You trade a little quality for large gains in cost and latency.
example: A large model's labels on 50,000 examples trained a small classifier that matched it within 2 points at a fraction of the per-request cost and a tenth of the latency.
diagram:
large model → labels on a big unlabelled set
  ↓ train the small model on those labels
small model: ~95% of the quality,
             a fraction of cost and latency

Best for narrow, high-volume tasks
how:
A large model is accurate and expensive. A small model is cheap and worse. Distillation narrows that gap for a specific task.

Run the large model over a large set of unlabelled examples and keep its outputs. Then train the small model to reproduce them. The small model is learning from a far richer signal than raw labels — it's learning the large model's behaviour on exactly the distribution you care about.

For a narrow, well-defined task, a distilled small model routinely reaches most of the large model's quality at a fraction of the cost and latency.

The constraint is scope. Distillation transfers behaviour on the distribution you distilled over. It does not produce a small general-purpose model, and performance falls away sharply outside that distribution.
more: It's most valuable for high-volume classification and extraction, where the same narrow task runs millions of times and the cost difference is enormous. Check the licence terms of the model you're distilling from — several providers restrict using outputs to train competing models, and that's a legal question rather than a technical one.
diagram2:
large model → outputs on 50,000 unlabelled examples
  ↓ train the small model to reproduce them
small model: ~95% of the quality
             a fraction of cost and latency ✓

Works because the small model learns behaviour
on exactly YOUR distribution.

Falls off sharply outside it —
this is not a small general-purpose model.

Check the provider's terms before distilling.

means: The process turning raw examples into trustworthy labelled data: sampling, guidelines, annotation, adjudication, and versioning of the result.
example: Labels collected ad hoc in a spreadsheet with no guidelines or version can't be trusted or reproduced. A pipeline makes the dataset an auditable artifact.
diagram:
sample (stratified, not just the easy cases)
  ↓ guidelines + worked examples
  ↓ annotate (2x on a subset for agreement)
  ↓ adjudicate disagreements
  ↓ version and freeze the dataset
how:
Labels collected ad hoc — a spreadsheet, a few people, no written guidance — can't be trusted or reproduced. A pipeline turns labelling into a repeatable process producing a versioned artifact.

The stages that matter: sample deliberately rather than taking whatever's convenient; write guidelines with worked examples including the hard cases; label, with a subset done twice so you can measure agreement; adjudicate disagreements and feed the resolution back into the guidelines; then freeze and version the result.

Sampling is where most datasets go wrong. Taking the first thousand records gives you a dataset dominated by the common case, and a model that scores well on it while failing on everything unusual.

Stratify: sample across document types, tenants, time periods and difficulty, deliberately over-representing the hard cases relative to their natural frequency.
more: Guidelines are a living document, not a preamble. Every adjudicated disagreement should produce a clarification with a worked example, so the same ambiguity isn't re-litigated by the next annotator. A mature guideline document is mostly edge cases, and that's a sign of health rather than complexity.
diagram2:
sample (stratified, hard cases over-represented)
  ↓ guidelines with worked examples
  ↓ label — a subset twice, for agreement
  ↓ adjudicate disagreements
  ↓ feed resolutions BACK into the guidelines
  ↓ freeze and version the dataset

First 1,000 records = the common case only
  → scores well, fails on everything unusual ✗

Mature guidelines are mostly edge cases.
That is health, not complexity.

means: Periodically consolidating an agent's accumulated memory — deduplicating, resolving contradictions, dropping the stale — so it doesn't grow into noise.
example: An assistant's memory held both 'user prefers email' and 'user prefers Slack' from different months. Compaction resolved to the most recent and dropped the stale entry.
diagram:
raw memories accumulate
  ↓ dedupe, resolve contradictions (recency wins),
    expire the stale, merge related
  ↓ compact, current memory

Without it: contradictory context,
            confidently wrong personalisation
how:
An agent that accumulates memories indefinitely ends up with a store that's contradictory, stale and mostly noise.

The problems compound. The same fact gets recorded several times in slightly different forms. A preference stated in March is contradicted in September and both remain. Facts tied to a completed task stay relevant-looking forever. And retrieval quality falls as the store fills with near-duplicates.

Compaction is a periodic pass that consolidates: deduplicate equivalent memories, resolve contradictions with recency winning by default, expire anything tied to finished work, and merge related entries into single coherent facts.

Without it, personalisation degrades into confident wrongness — which users experience as worse than no memory at all, because the system is acting on something it believes about them that isn't true.
more: Keep the compaction decisions auditable — what was merged, what was dropped, what superseded what. When a user asks why the assistant believes something about them, you need an answer, and in some jurisdictions they have a right to one. An opaque memory store is difficult to explain and difficult to correct.
diagram2:
Accumulated raw:
  "prefers email"       (March)
  "prefers Slack"       (September)
  "prefers email"       (March, duplicate)
  "needs the Q2 file"   (task finished in April)

Compaction:
  dedupe · recency resolves contradictions
  expire task-scoped facts · merge related entries
  ↓
  "prefers Slack" ✓

Without it: confident wrongness,
which users like less than no memory at all.

Keep the decisions auditable.

means: Purpose-built inference servers implementing continuous batching, paged KV cache and optimised kernels. Naive serving loops leave most of the hardware unused.
example: A hand-rolled FastAPI wrapper around a model served a fraction of the throughput vLLM achieved on identical hardware, purely from batching and KV cache management.
diagram:
naive loop: one request at a time, idle GPU
vLLM/TGI:   continuous batching, paged KV cache,
            optimised kernels, streaming

Same GPU, several times the throughput.
Don't hand-roll this.
how:
Wrapping a model in a web framework and calling it per request is the obvious approach and leaves most of the hardware unused.

Purpose-built inference servers implement several things that are individually difficult. Continuous batching, so finished sequences free their slot immediately. Paged attention, which manages KV cache memory in pages rather than contiguous blocks, dramatically reducing waste. Optimised kernels for the specific operations transformers perform. Efficient scheduling across concurrent requests.

Together these routinely deliver several times the throughput of a naive loop on identical hardware.

Since throughput translates directly into GPU count, and GPUs dominate the cost of self-hosting, the choice of serving stack is one of the larger cost decisions available — and it's a configuration choice, not an engineering project.
more: This only applies to self-hosting. If you're calling a provider API, they've solved it and the equivalent decision for you is batching, caching and routing. Knowing why the numbers differ is still useful — it explains why per-token pricing varies so much between providers and model sizes.
diagram2:
Naive: FastAPI wrapper, one request at a time
  → most of the GPU idle

vLLM / TGI / Triton:
  ├ continuous batching (slots freed per step)
  ├ paged attention (KV cache in pages)
  ├ optimised transformer kernels
  └ concurrent scheduling

Several times the throughput, same hardware.
Throughput → GPU count → the bulk of your bill.

A configuration choice, not a project.
Only relevant if you self-host.

means: Removing chunks that are near-identical, so retrieval doesn't spend its budget returning the same passage five times.
example: A policy paragraph repeated across 40 documents filled the top 5 results with copies. MinHash dedup at ingest freed those slots for different information.
diagram:
exact dedup:  hash the content
near dedup:   MinHash / SimHash / embedding cosine

top-5 results = 5 copies of one passage ✗
after dedup   = 5 distinct sources ✓
how:
Corpora accumulate repetition. The same policy paragraph appears in forty documents, a template header repeats across every contract, a page exists in three revisions of the same file.

Retrieval doesn't know these are duplicates. Ask a question that matches that repeated paragraph and your top five results are five copies of it. You've spent the entire retrieval budget on one piece of information, and the model has no other sources to work from.

Exact duplicates are trivial — hash the content. Near-duplicates are the real problem: same text with a different date, a reformatted version, one changed sentence.

Those need similarity detection. MinHash or SimHash catch near-identical text cheaply; embedding cosine above a high threshold catches semantic repetition at more cost.
more: Where duplicates are legitimately distinct — the same clause in two different contracts, both of which matter — deduplicate at retrieval time rather than at ingest. Keep everything indexed, then collapse near-identical results after ranking so the top k contains k distinct pieces of information. You keep the coverage and lose the redundancy.
diagram2:
query matches a paragraph repeated 40 times
  → top 5 results = 5 copies of it
  → the model has one source, not five ✗

exact:  content hash
near:   MinHash / SimHash (cheap)
        embedding cosine > 0.97 (semantic)

If the duplicates are legitimately distinct
(same clause, two different contracts):
  keep both indexed
  dedupe AFTER ranking
  → top k = k distinct pieces of information ✓

means: Asking which of two outputs is better, rather than scoring one in isolation. People and judges are far more reliable at comparison than at absolute rating.
example: Rating answers 1-5 produced almost everything as a 4. Showing A and B side by side gave a clear, stable preference signal and a usable win rate.
diagram:
"rate 1-5"  → everything is a 4, no signal
"A or B?"   → clear win rate ✓

Randomise position (position bias is real)
Report: win / loss / tie, with confidence
how:
Asking anyone — human or model — to rate an answer from 1 to 5 produces poor data. Most things land on 4, the scale drifts between sessions, and two reviewers mean different things by 3.

Comparison is far more reliable. Show two outputs and ask which is better. That question has a stable answer, needs no calibration, and both humans and judge models are noticeably more consistent at it.

You lose absolute magnitude — a win rate tells you A beats B 68% of the time, not by how much. In practice that's what you needed anyway, because the decision is which to ship.

The essential control is randomising which option appears first. Position bias is real and large enough to manufacture a result if you always show the new version second.
more: Report the win rate with ties counted separately, and with a confidence interval. Thirty comparisons splitting 17-13 is noise, and treating it as a result is how teams convince themselves a neutral change was an improvement. If you can't run enough comparisons to distinguish the two, that itself is the finding: the change doesn't matter much.
diagram2:
"Rate 1-5"     → everything is a 4, no signal
"A or B?"      → stable, consistent ✓

Report:
  A wins 62% · B wins 28% · tie 10%
  n = 200, CI ±7%

Controls:
  randomise position every comparison
  (position bias alone can flip a result)

17-13 out of 30 is not a result.
It means the change doesn't matter much.

means: Pre-populating caches for known-hot queries after a deploy or index swap, so users don't all pay the cold cost at once.
example: After every index rebuild the first thousand users saw 900ms retrieval. Replaying the top 500 queries first made the swap invisible.
diagram:
index swap / deploy
  ↓ replay the top-N historical queries
  ↓ caches populated before real traffic arrives

Otherwise every rebuild is a small self-inflicted incident
how:
Caches make a retrieval system fast, and they're empty after every deploy, index swap or restart.

The result is a burst of degraded performance exactly when you least want it. The first few hundred users after a rebuild pay full uncached cost — vector search, reranking, sometimes an embedding call for the query — while everyone afterwards gets the fast path.

Warming replays the most common historical queries against the new state before real traffic arrives, so the caches are populated by the time users show up.

It's a small amount of work that converts a visible periodic degradation into a non-event. On systems that rebuild frequently it's the difference between users noticing your deploys and not.
more: Warm on the real query distribution, taken from logs, rather than a hand-written list. The queries you'd write are the ones you think are important; the ones in the logs are the ones actually asked. A few hundred of the most frequent typically covers a large share of traffic, because query distributions are heavily skewed.
diagram2:
index swap / deploy / restart
  → caches empty
  → first few hundred users pay full cost
  → then everyone else is fast

Every rebuild = a small self-inflicted incident.

Warm before opening traffic:
  replay the top N historical queries
  from LOGS, not from a hand-written list

Query distributions are heavily skewed —
a few hundred queries covers most traffic.

means: Training a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimising the policy against it. The technique that made assistants feel aligned with intent.
example: Humans rank pairs of outputs, a reward model learns to predict those rankings, and the policy is optimised against that reward — with a penalty for drifting too far from the base.
diagram:
collect preference pairs (A better than B)
  ↓ train a reward model
  ↓ optimise the policy against the reward
  ↓ KL penalty keeps it near the base model

Failure mode: the policy games the reward model
how:
You can't write a loss function for "helpful". So RLHF learns one from human judgement instead.

Three stages. First, collect comparisons: show humans two model outputs for the same prompt and record which they preferred. Second, train a reward model on those comparisons — a model whose job is predicting which output a human would choose. Third, optimise the main model to produce outputs the reward model scores highly.

A constraint keeps this from going off the rails: a penalty for drifting too far from the original model. Without it the policy finds outputs that score enormously well and read as gibberish.

That's reward hacking, and it's the characteristic failure — the model optimising the proxy rather than the thing the proxy was meant to represent.
more: You almost certainly won't run RLHF, and it's worth understanding anyway, because its fingerprints are on the models you use. Traits like verbosity, hedging and eagerness to please are partly artifacts of what human raters preferred during this phase. Knowing that explains behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary.
diagram2:
1. humans compare pairs → preference data
2. train a reward model to predict preferences
3. optimise the policy against that reward
   + KL penalty to stay near the base model

Without the penalty:
  the policy finds high-scoring gibberish
  → reward hacking: optimising the proxy ✗

Why you care even without running it:
  verbosity, hedging, eagerness to please
  are partly artifacts of this phase.

means: Accounting for weights, KV cache and activations, because the KV cache grows with concurrency times context length and is what actually causes OOM.
example: A 13B model in fp16 is ~26GB of weights. On an 80GB card the remaining ~50GB caps how many long-context requests can be in flight at once.
diagram:
VRAM = weights + KV cache + activations + overhead

KV cache ∝ batch × context length × layers
  ↓
Long contexts collapse your max concurrency
Set max_model_len and max_num_seqs deliberately
how:
Self-hosting requires knowing what occupies GPU memory, because running out is a crash rather than a slowdown.

Three consumers. Model weights: fixed and easy to calculate — roughly two bytes per parameter at 16-bit precision, so a 13B model is about 26GB. Activations: transient working memory during a forward pass. And the KV cache, which is where the difficulty lives.

The KV cache scales with sequence length multiplied by how many requests are in flight. It's not fixed — it grows as conversations get longer and as concurrency rises.

Which produces the counterintuitive operational property: a server comfortably handling sixty short conversations can fall over on eight long ones, at identical request rates, because the memory profile is completely different.
more: Set explicit limits — maximum sequence length and maximum concurrent sequences — so the server rejects or queues rather than exhausting memory. An out-of-memory crash takes down every in-flight request; a queue delays one. Modern serving stacks manage this well with paged attention, but you still have to give them the bounds.
diagram2:
VRAM = weights + activations + KV cache

weights   13B model at fp16 ≈ 26GB (fixed)
KV cache  ∝ sequence length × concurrent requests
          ↑ this is what actually OOMs you

Counterintuitive:
  60 short conversations → fine
   8 long conversations  → OOM
  same request rate, different memory profile

Set max_model_len and max_num_seqs.
OOM kills every in-flight request. A queue delays one.

means: Models attend most reliably to the beginning and end of a long context. Material buried in the middle is measurably more likely to be missed.
example: The critical clause sits at position 40 of 60 retrieved chunks and the model misses it. Reranking to 5 chunks with the best first fixed the answer.
diagram:
attention reliability across position:
  start ████████  strong
  middle ███      weak ← things get lost here
  end   ███████   strong

Fewer, better-ordered chunks beat more chunks
how:
Models advertise very large context windows, and it's natural to assume that all of it works equally well. Measurement says otherwise.

If you place a specific fact somewhere in a long context and then ask about it, retrieval accuracy depends strongly on where you put it. Facts near the beginning and near the end are found reliably. Facts in the middle are missed noticeably more often. This pattern shows up consistently across models and is often called "lost in the middle".

The practical consequence is that a large context window is a capacity limit, not a promise of attention. Filling it because you can actively hurts you.

Retrieving forty chunks so that the right one is definitely in there is a false comfort if the model then overlooks it in position twenty-three.
more: This is why reranking pays for itself so consistently in RAG systems. Fewer, better-ordered chunks outperform more chunks almost every time. The practical pattern is to retrieve broadly for recall, rerank down to a handful, and place the strongest material at the start and end of the context rather than burying it in a long undifferentiated list.
diagram2:
Reliability of retrieval by position:

  start   ████████  strong
  middle  ███       weaker ← things get missed
  end     ███████   strong

40 chunks retrieved, the answer sits at #23
  → often overlooked

5 reranked chunks, best first
  → found reliably ✓

Big window = capacity, not attention.
reason: coined term, not in common use

means: A vector representing meaning, where similar text lands close together. The foundation of semantic search, clustering and dedup.
example: 'How do I reset my password?' and 'forgot login credentials' share almost no keywords but have high cosine similarity, so semantic search finds both.
diagram:
text → model → [0.02, -0.41, ..., 0.18] (1536d)

   "reset my password"
          ●
         ╱ small angle → cosine 0.94
        ●  "forgot login credentials"


                    ● "shipment delayed"
                      cosine 0.11

No shared keywords, still close.
Same model for documents AND queries, always.
how:
An embedding is a list of numbers — often 1,536 of them — that represents the meaning of a piece of text.

The property that makes this useful: texts meaning similar things produce number lists that point in similar directions, even when they share no words at all. "Reset my password" and "forgot my login" have almost no vocabulary in common and sit very close together.

That's the entire basis of semantic search. Instead of matching words, you convert everything to vectors once, then find the nearest ones to your query's vector.

The rule that trips people up: the numbers only mean anything relative to the model that produced them. Vectors from two different models — or two versions of one model — are not comparable. Mixing them silently returns nonsense rather than raising an error.
more: A limitation worth knowing early: embeddings capture topical similarity, not logical relationships. "The contract was signed" and "the contract was not signed" embed very close together, because they're about the same thing. Negation, numbers and exact identifiers are all weak points — which is precisely why hybrid search, combining embeddings with keyword matching, outperforms either one alone.
diagram2:
text → embedding model → [0.02, -0.41, ..., 0.18]

  "reset my password"
        ●
       ╱ close → cosine 0.94
      ●  "forgot my login"       ● "shipping delay"
                                   cosine 0.11
No shared words. Still close. ✓

Weak points:
  "signed" vs "not signed"  → nearly identical ✗
  invoice code "ERR_4471"   → no neighbours ✗
                              (use keyword search)

means: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and is compute-bound. Decode generates one token at a time and is memory-bandwidth-bound. Different bottlenecks, different fixes.
example: Long prompts hurt TTFT (prefill). Long outputs hurt total time (decode). Batching helps decode throughput a lot and prefill much less.
diagram:
Prefill: all prompt tokens at once
  compute-bound → GPU FLOPs
Decode: 1 token at a time, sequential
  memory-bandwidth-bound → batching helps

Optimise the one that's actually your bottleneck
how:
Inference has two phases with completely different performance characteristics, and confusing them means optimising the wrong thing.

Prefill reads your prompt. Every token can be processed at the same time, in parallel, because they're all already known. That keeps the GPU's arithmetic units busy — it's compute-bound.

Decode writes the answer. It cannot be parallelised, because token 2 depends on token 1 existing. So the GPU does a small amount of arithmetic, then waits while the model's weights are read from memory, over and over. It's memory-bandwidth-bound, and the expensive silicon spends most of its time idle.

That asymmetry is why batching helps so much: while one request waits on memory, others can use the idle compute.
more: Diagnostically: if long prompts hurt, you're prefill-bound — cut input tokens. If long answers hurt, you're decode-bound — cut output tokens, or batch more aggressively. Buying a faster GPU helps prefill considerably and decode much less, because decode is limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw arithmetic speed.
diagram2:
PREFILL — all prompt tokens at once
  [t1][t2][t3]...[t2000]  → parallel ✓
  compute-bound, GPU busy

DECODE — one token at a time
  [t1] → wait → [t2] → wait → [t3]
  memory-bandwidth-bound, GPU mostly idle
       ↑ batching fills this idle time

means: Storing weights at lower precision (int8, int4) to cut memory and increase speed, at some quality cost.
example: A 70B model in fp16 needs ~140GB; at int4 it's ~35GB and fits one GPU. Quality drops slightly and is very task-dependent — measure, don't assume.
diagram:
fp16  140GB  baseline quality
int8   70GB  ~lossless for most tasks
int4   35GB  noticeable on hard reasoning

Always eval your own task after quantising
how:
Model weights are numbers. By default each is stored in 16 bits. Quantisation stores them in fewer — 8 bits, or 4.

Two things improve at once. Memory drops proportionally, so a model that needed two GPUs might fit on one. And speed improves, because decode is limited by how fast weights can be read from memory — smaller weights means less to read.

The cost is precision. Each weight is now an approximation, and those small errors accumulate through the network.

What matters in practice is that the damage is very uneven across tasks. Summarisation and casual chat often survive 4-bit almost untouched. Multi-step arithmetic, careful instruction-following and structured output degrade noticeably. The average benchmark hides this, because it averages the tasks that broke with the ones that didn't.
more: So the rule is simple and non-negotiable: never accept a quantised model on someone else's benchmark. Run your own evaluation set against both versions on your own task. The decision is usually clear within an hour, and skipping that hour is how teams ship a quality regression they can't explain three weeks later.
diagram2:
A 70B model:

fp16   ~140GB   baseline quality
int8    ~70GB   usually near-lossless
int4    ~35GB   fits one GPU, task-dependent loss

Survives well:   summarising, chat, extraction
Degrades first:  arithmetic, long reasoning,
                 strict format adherence

means: A small draft model proposes several tokens, the large model verifies them in one pass. Same output distribution, fewer expensive forward passes.
example: A 1B draft model proposes 4 tokens; the 70B accepts 3. You produced 3 tokens for roughly one large-model step — often a 2-3x speedup.
diagram:
draft model → proposes 4 tokens
large model → verifies in ONE pass
  accepted 3, rejected 1 → resume from there

2-3x faster, identical output distribution
how:
Decode is slow because tokens must be produced one at a time, each requiring a full pass through a very large model.

The insight behind speculative decoding is that most tokens are easy. After "the capital of France is", almost any model knows what follows. You don't need 70 billion parameters for that.

So you run a small, fast draft model to guess the next several tokens. Then the large model checks all of those guesses in a single pass — and checking several tokens at once is nearly as cheap as generating one, because that pass is memory-bound rather than compute-bound.

Guesses that match what the large model would have produced are kept. The first mismatch is corrected and drafting resumes from there.
more: The property that makes this safe is that the output distribution is mathematically identical to running the large model alone. This is not an approximation and it is not a quality trade-off — it is the same output, produced with fewer expensive passes. The gain depends on how often the draft model guesses right, which is high for predictable text and low for genuinely novel content.
diagram2:
Draft model proposes:  " the capital of Spain"
Large model verifies in ONE pass:
                        ✓    ✓       ✓     ✗
                                            └ corrected

3 tokens accepted for the cost of ~1 large pass
Typical speedup 2-3x. Output distribution unchanged.

means: Sending tokens as they're generated. It doesn't make anything faster; it makes waiting tolerable and lets users bail early.
example: A 12-second response streamed feels responsive. The same 12 seconds behind a spinner feels broken. Users also stop reading early and cancel, saving tokens.
diagram:
Non-streaming: [====== 12s blank ======] answer
Streaming:     [0.4s] tokens flowing...

Same total time, completely different UX
Also enables early cancellation
how:
Streaming sends tokens to the client as they're produced, instead of waiting for the complete response and sending it at once.

It's worth being precise about what this does and doesn't do. Total generation time is unchanged. Nothing is faster. What changes is that the user sees progress immediately rather than staring at a spinner.

That distinction matters because perceived performance and actual performance are genuinely different things, and users only experience the first one. A twelve-second streamed response feels responsive. Twelve seconds of nothing followed by the same text feels broken.

There's a real efficiency gain too: users frequently see enough in the first few lines to know the answer isn't what they wanted, and cancel. Those cancelled tokens are never generated, so you don't pay for them.
more: The engineering cost is that error handling gets harder. Once you've sent a 200 status and started streaming, you cannot retract it — a failure halfway through arrives as a truncated answer rather than a clean error. Design for that explicitly: send a terminal event that marks success, so the client can tell "finished" from "connection died", and decide in advance whether a partial answer is shown or discarded.
diagram2:
NON-STREAMING
  [========= 12s of nothing =========] full answer
  feels broken

STREAMING
  [0.4s] first tokens → text flowing → done at 12s
  feels responsive

Same 12 seconds. Different product.

Watch: a mid-stream failure looks like a
       short answer, not like an error.
       Always send an explicit done event.

means: The unit models actually read and bill on. Roughly 4 characters of English, and far less efficient for code, JSON and Indic scripts.
example: A 10,000-word English document is about 13,000 tokens. The same content in Hindi can be 2-3x more, which quietly changes both cost and context fit.
diagram:
"unbelievable" → ["un","bel","iev","able"]

English    ~4 chars/token
Code/JSON  ~2-3 chars/token
Hindi/Tamil ~1-2 chars/token ← costs multiply
how:
Models don't read characters and they don't read words. Before anything happens, your text is chopped into tokens by a tokeniser — a fixed vocabulary of maybe 100,000 pieces, learned once when the model was built. Common words are one token. Rare words get split into fragments.

Why should you care? Because tokens are the unit of everything you pay for and everything you're limited by. Context windows are measured in tokens. Bills are per token. Speed is tokens per second.

The trap is that the tokeniser was trained mostly on English prose, so that's what it compresses best. Anything unusual — code, JSON, UUIDs, non-Latin scripts — splits into far more pieces than you'd guess from its length.
more: A practical consequence: the same information costs different amounts depending on how you format it. A deeply nested JSON blob spends a lot of tokens on braces, quotes and repeated key names. The same data as a compact table or as plain sentences can be meaningfully cheaper, and the model often reads it just as well. When a prompt is large and stable, this is worth measuring rather than assuming.
diagram2:
Rough cost of the same content:

English prose      1,000 words → ~1,300 tokens
JSON, nested       1,000 words → ~2,500 tokens
Code               1,000 words → ~2,000 tokens
Hindi / Tamil      1,000 words → ~3,000+ tokens

Never estimate by character count. Measure.

means: Generation speed. Below reading speed the stream feels like a drip; well above it, users can't tell the difference.
example: 80 tokens/sec streams faster than most people read and feels smooth. At 5 tokens/sec the same response is agonising even though the content is identical.
diagram:
80 tok/s → smooth, ahead of reading ✓
20 tok/s → noticeable lag
5  tok/s → frustrating drip ✗

Per-user throughput ≠ fleet throughput
how:
Tokens per second — how fast text appears once it has started.

The number to compare it against is human reading speed, which is roughly 4-8 tokens per second for careful reading. Anything comfortably above that means the user is never waiting on the model; they're limited by their own reading.

That gives you a useful threshold. Going from 20 to 80 tokens per second is a large, obvious improvement. Going from 80 to 160 is mostly invisible, because nobody reads that fast.

One distinction that causes real confusion: per-request throughput and total system throughput are different numbers and they trade against each other. Larger batches raise total tokens served across all users while each individual user's stream gets slightly slower.
more: Which one you optimise depends on the product. An interactive chat should protect per-user speed. A background job classifying ten million documents should maximise total throughput and not care that any individual document takes longer. Serving both workloads from one pool with one configuration means neither gets what it needs.
diagram2:
Reading speed ≈ 4-8 tok/s

  5 tok/s  ▪ ▪ ▪ ▪    painful drip
 20 tok/s  ▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪   acceptable
 80 tok/s  ████████   ahead of reading ✓
160 tok/s  ████████   ...no different to the user

Interactive → protect per-user speed
Batch job   → maximise total throughput

means: Repeating a slice of the previous chunk so meaning spanning a boundary survives. Costs storage and creates near-duplicate results.
example: A 15% overlap keeps the sentence that straddled the split. Push it to 50% and your top-5 results are three copies of the same passage.
diagram:
[chunk 1: 0-500]
        [chunk 2: 425-925]  ← 15% overlap
                [chunk 3: 850-1350]

Too little → lost context
Too much → duplicate results, wasted context
how:
Even good chunk boundaries cut some ideas in half. Overlap is the cheap insurance: each chunk repeats the last slice of the one before it.

So if a definition spans a boundary, the second chunk still carries the opening of it, and the passage remains retrievable and readable.

The cost is duplication. Every overlapped token is stored twice, embedded twice, and — most importantly — can be returned twice. Push overlap high and your top five results become three copies of the same passage wearing different boundaries, which wastes both context budget and the model's attention.

Ten to twenty percent is the range most systems settle on. Past that you're usually papering over a chunking strategy that should be fixed properly.
more: Overlap and chunk size interact. Small chunks retrieve precisely but lose surrounding context, so they need proportionally more overlap. Large chunks carry their own context but dilute the embedding, since one vector now has to represent several ideas at once. Tune them together against a retrieval evaluation set, not separately by intuition.
diagram2:
[ chunk 1  0-500 ]
        [ chunk 2  425-925 ]     ← 15% overlap
                [ chunk 3  850-1350 ]

Too little  → ideas cut in half, unretrievable
Too much    → top-5 is the same passage ×3
              context budget wasted

Small chunks → more overlap needed
Large chunks → diluted embedding

means: Cosine measures angle only; dot product also rewards magnitude. Mixing the wrong metric with your index configuration silently degrades results.
example: Switching an index from cosine to dot product without renormalising made longer documents rank higher regardless of relevance.
diagram:
cosine = dot / (|a|·|b|)   → angle only
dot    = raw                → magnitude matters

Normalised vectors → they're equivalent
Index metric must match how you embedded
how:
Both measure how alike two vectors are, and they differ in whether length counts.

Picture each embedding as an arrow from the origin. Cosine similarity looks only at the angle between two arrows — pure direction, length ignored. Dot product multiplies the components, so a longer arrow scores higher regardless of direction.

For meaning, direction is what you want. Length in an embedding tends to correlate with things you don't care about, like how long the source text was. Using dot product on unnormalised vectors quietly ranks longer documents above shorter, more relevant ones.

There's a shortcut most systems use: normalise every vector to length 1 when you store it. Once all arrows are the same length, dot product and cosine become mathematically identical, and dot product is cheaper to compute.
more: The failure mode to watch for is a mismatch between how you embedded and how your index is configured to compare. Change an index from cosine to dot product without renormalising, or switch embedding models to one that doesn't normalise by default, and nothing errors — results just get subtly worse. Record the metric alongside the vectors and assert it on startup.
diagram2:
cosine = angle only, length ignored
dot    = angle AND length

  short, highly relevant doc   → shorter arrow
  long, vaguely relevant doc   → longer arrow

dot product on unnormalised vectors
  → ranks the long vague one higher ✗

Normalise to length 1 at write time
  → cosine and dot become identical ✓
  → and dot is cheaper

means: IVF clusters vectors and only searches the nearest clusters. PQ compresses vectors so far more fit in RAM, with some precision loss.
example: 100M vectors at 1536 dims in float32 is ~600GB. PQ compresses it to ~20GB, making a single-machine index feasible at some recall cost.
diagram:
IVF: cluster → search nprobe nearest clusters
PQ:  split vector into sub-vectors → codebook

float32 1536d = 6KB/vector → 600GB at 100M
PQ compressed = ~200B/vector → 20GB ✓
how:
These are two different savings, often used together.

IVF (inverted file) is about search effort. Cluster all your vectors into, say, 4,096 groups and store which group each belongs to. At query time, work out which few groups your query is nearest and search only those. You've skipped the vast majority of the data.

Product quantisation is about memory. A 1,536-dimension vector in 32-bit floats is about 6KB. PQ chops the vector into small sub-vectors, and replaces each with the ID of the nearest entry in a small learned codebook. You store a handful of IDs instead of thousands of floats — often a 30x reduction.

That reduction is what turns an impossible index into a feasible one. A hundred million vectors is roughly 600GB raw and roughly 20GB with PQ, and the second one fits on a single machine.
more: PQ is lossy, so distances computed from compressed vectors are approximations of approximations. The standard mitigation is a two-stage search: use the compressed vectors to shortlist candidates fast, then rescore that shortlist against full-precision vectors for the final ranking. You get most of the memory saving and most of the accuracy back.
diagram2:
IVF — search less
  4,096 clusters, probe the nearest 8
  → ~0.2% of the data examined

PQ — store less
  1,536 floats × 4 bytes = 6,144 bytes
  → 96 codebook IDs      =    96 bytes

100M vectors: 600GB → ~20GB ✓

Combine, then rescore the shortlist
against full-precision vectors.

means: Keeping tenants' vectors isolated. Getting this wrong leaks one customer's documents into another's answers — the worst bug this stack can produce.
example: A shared index with metadata filtering is efficient but one missing filter leaks data. Namespaces or per-tenant collections make leakage structurally impossible.
diagram:
Shared index + filter → efficient, one bug = leak ✗
Namespace per tenant  → isolated ✓
Collection per tenant → strongest, scaling limits

Enforce the tenant filter in a shared data layer,
never in each call site
how:
If one customer's documents can surface in another customer's answers, you have the worst bug this stack can produce. It's not a quality regression — it's a data breach, and it's usually silent.

The tempting design is one shared index with a tenant_id in the metadata, filtered at query time. Efficient, simple, and it means correctness depends on every single query remembering the filter. One code path that forgets — a debugging endpoint, a batch job, a new feature written in a hurry — and the isolation is gone with no error raised.

The safer design makes leakage structurally impossible instead of procedurally avoided. Namespaces or per-tenant collections mean the tenant determines *which index you search*, so there's no filter to forget.

You're choosing between an invariant enforced by discipline and one enforced by architecture.
more: If you must share an index, at minimum force every query through one data-access layer that injects the tenant filter, so no call site can construct a raw query. Then test it adversarially: seed two tenants with deliberately similar documents and assert that neither can retrieve the other's, as a permanent test rather than a one-off check.
diagram2:
SHARED INDEX + FILTER
  every query must remember the filter
  one forgotten filter = cross-tenant leak
  no error, no log line, silent ✗

NAMESPACE PER TENANT
  the tenant chooses the index
  nothing to forget ✓

Minimum if sharing:
  one data-access layer injects the filter
  adversarial test: tenant A cannot see B

means: Prompting the model to reason step by step before answering. Helps multi-step problems, costs tokens, and reasoning models do it natively.
example: Adding step-by-step reasoning to a multi-hop question raised accuracy from 62% to 84% and tripled output tokens. Worth it there, waste on classification.
diagram:
direct:         question → answer (62%)
step-by-step:   question → reasoning → answer (84%)

Cost: 3x output tokens
Reasoning models do this internally — don't double up
how:
The model produces one token at a time, and each token is a fixed amount of computation. It cannot pause and think harder before answering.

That constraint explains why chain of thought works. Asking for reasoning steps before the answer gives the model more tokens to work through the problem — the intermediate steps become scratch space, and each one conditions what comes next. Rather than jumping straight to a conclusion, it builds toward one.

The gains are real on multi-step problems: arithmetic, logic, anything requiring several dependent inferences. They're negligible on single-step tasks like classification or extraction, where there's nothing to reason through and you've just paid for extra tokens.

Newer reasoning models do this internally, so explicitly prompting for it duplicates work and can make output worse.
more: One caution that matters for trust: the stated reasoning is not necessarily the actual mechanism. Models can produce plausible-looking reasoning that doesn't correspond to how they arrived at the answer, including reasoning that confidently supports a wrong conclusion. Treat it as useful for debugging and unreliable as evidence — a well-argued chain of thought is not proof the answer is right.
diagram2:
Direct:
  "What's 17% of 4,280?"  → "$727.60"  ✗

Step by step:
  10% = 428
  7%  = 299.6
  total = 727.6                        ✓

Multi-step reasoning  → 62% → 84%
Classification        → no change, 3x tokens

Reasoning models: already internal.
Prompting for it again can hurt.

means: Showing examples of the input-output mapping instead of describing it. Usually beats a longer prose instruction for format adherence.
example: Three worked examples of the exact JSON shape produced more consistent output than two paragraphs describing the schema.
diagram:
instruction only     → 78% format adherence
+ 3 worked examples  → 96% ✓

Examples should cover edge cases,
not just the happy path
how:
Instead of describing what you want, show two or three worked examples of input and correct output. The model infers the pattern.

This works better than description for anything with a shape — a JSON schema, a classification label set, a particular tone — because an example is unambiguous in ways prose isn't. Two paragraphs explaining your output format leave room for interpretation. Three examples of it do not.

The choice of examples is where the quality is. Three examples of the easy, typical case teach the model the easy case. Examples that cover the edges — the ambiguous input, the one where the correct answer is "none of these", the malformed record — teach it what to do when things get difficult, which is precisely where it would otherwise improvise.

Pick them from cases your system got wrong.
more: Few-shot examples are pure input tokens, paid on every request. Once the model reliably follows the format, test removing them one at a time — often the quality holds with two examples instead of six, and you've cut a meaningful slice of your input cost. If they're staying, put them in the cached prefix.

Instruction only:

  → 78% format adherence

+ 3 examples covering edges:
  a normal case
  an ambiguous case
  a case where the answer is null
  → 96% adherence ✓

Examples are input tokens, every request.
Trim once the format is stable. Cache the rest.

means: The stable instruction layer defining role, constraints and output format. It is not a security boundary — users can often infer or override it.
example: Keeping the system prompt stable and putting variable content after it maximises prompt-cache hits and makes A/B testing meaningful.
diagram:
system: role, rules, format, tools (stable)
history: prior turns
user:    this request (variable)

Stable content first → cache hits
Never put secrets here — treat it as visible
how:
The system prompt is the block of instructions sent ahead of the conversation on every request. It sets role, constraints, output format and available tools.

Two things about it are widely misunderstood.

It is not persistent. There is no memory on the provider's side. Your application resends it in full on every single call, which is why it dominates input cost on high-traffic endpoints.

And it is not a security boundary. It's text in the same stream as everything else, and the model weighs it against everything else. It can be talked around, and its contents can usually be extracted by a determined user. Anything you'd be unhappy to see published should not be in it — no credentials, no internal URLs, no descriptions of undisclosed features.
more: Because it's resent every time and sits at the very front of the input, it's also your best prompt-caching opportunity. Keep it genuinely stable — no timestamps, no per-user interpolation, no request IDs — and put variable content after it. A single dynamic value at the top of a 10,000-token system prompt disables caching for every request.

[ system prompt ][ history ][ retrieved ][ user ]
  ↑ resent in full, every single request
  ↑ front of input → prime cache territory

Do NOT put here:
  API keys · internal hostnames · secrets
  anything you'd mind a user extracting

Do NOT interpolate here:
  timestamps · user names · request IDs
  → each one is a cache miss

means: Converting to black and white before recognition. Adaptive thresholding handles uneven lighting that a global threshold destroys.
example: A phone photo with a shadow across half the page loses that half entirely with global thresholding. Adaptive (Sauvola) keeps both halves readable.
diagram:
global threshold  → shadowed half turns black ✗
adaptive (per-region) → both halves readable ✓

Also: denoise, contrast, upscale small text
how:
Recognition works best on clean black text against white, so a colour or greyscale image is usually converted to pure black and white first. Binarisation is choosing, per pixel, which it becomes.

A global threshold picks one brightness cutoff for the whole image. That works on an evenly lit scan and fails badly on anything photographed. A shadow across half a page means those pixels fall below the cutoff and the entire region turns solid black — text and background together, unrecoverable.

Adaptive methods compute a threshold per small region instead, so each part of the image is judged against its own local brightness. The shadowed half gets a lower cutoff, and its text survives.

For phone-captured documents — which is most real-world input now — adaptive is not an optimisation, it's the difference between working and not.
more: Modern deep-learning OCR is often trained on greyscale and can be hurt by aggressive binarisation, which destroys information about faint or thin strokes. Check which your engine expects before adding it. This is a good example of preprocessing advice aging: a step that was mandatory for older engines can be counterproductive for newer ones.

Photo with a shadow down one side:

Global threshold (one cutoff for the page):
  lit half     → text readable ✓
  shadowed half → entirely black, text lost ✗

Adaptive (threshold per local region):
  both halves judged against local brightness ✓

But check your engine first:
  classic OCR   → wants binarised input
  deep-learning → often wants greyscale;
                  binarising can lose thin strokes

means: Recognising handwriting, which is far harder than print. Cursive and free-form fields remain unreliable enough to need review.
example: Printed forms hit 98%. The same fields handwritten hit 76%, and cursive names much lower. Anything handwritten routes to review by default.
diagram:
printed text   ~98%
hand-printed   ~85%
cursive        ~60-75%

Design forms with boxes per character
if accuracy actually matters
how:
Handwriting is a substantially harder problem than print, and the gap doesn't close with a better model.

Printed text has a small number of consistent glyph shapes. Handwriting has as many variants as writers, letters connect to each other so segmentation is ambiguous, baselines wander, and the same person writes differently depending on speed and space.

Accuracy therefore splits sharply by style. Hand-printed characters in separated boxes approach print accuracy. Continuous cursive drops far enough that field-level review becomes mandatory.

The most useful implication is upstream of any technology choice: if you control the form, design it to be recognisable. Individual character boxes, clear field boundaries and generous spacing improve accuracy more than any model change available to you.
more: Proper nouns are the hardest category, because context can't rescue them. A model reading a handwritten sentence can infer an unclear word from its neighbours. A handwritten surname has no such context — it could be almost anything. Route names, addresses and reference codes to review by default regardless of confidence.

hand-printed

Form design beats model selection:
  ▢▢▢▢▢▢  one box per character
  clear field boundaries, generous spacing

Proper nouns have no context to recover from.

means: Correcting page rotation before recognition. A few degrees of tilt from a phone photo can cost double-digit accuracy.
example: Scanned pages at 3-5° tilt dropped accuracy from 96% to 71%. Deskewing as a preprocessing step restored it with no model change.
diagram:
tilted page → OCR accuracy 71%
  ↓ detect angle → rotate → deskew
straight page → 96% ✓

Preprocessing often beats a bigger model
how:
Recognition models expect text on horizontal baselines. Phone photographs and hand-fed scans routinely arrive a few degrees off.

A small tilt does more damage than intuition suggests. At three to five degrees, a line of text drifts vertically across the page — by the right margin it may overlap the line below. Line segmentation starts merging adjacent lines, and character recognition degrades sharply.

Deskewing detects the dominant angle — typically by finding the orientation at which horizontal projections of dark pixels are most sharply peaked — and rotates the image back.

It's one of the cheapest steps in the pipeline and one of the highest-return. Fixing input geometry routinely beats upgrading the recognition model, at a fraction of the cost.
more: It belongs to a family of preprocessing steps worth doing before blaming the model: deskew, denoise, correct uneven lighting, and upscale text that's too small for the engine's expected range. On phone-captured documents these together often move accuracy more than any model change available to you.

3-5° tilt:
  by the right margin, a line has drifted
  down far enough to overlap the next one
  → lines merge → characters degrade
  → accuracy 96% → 71% ✗

detect dominant angle → rotate back → 96% ✓

Preprocessing worth doing first:
  deskew · denoise · lighting · upscale small text

Cheaper and more effective than a bigger model.

means: Big Objects store billions of rows for archival with a very restricted query model — index-only filters, no triggers, no standard reporting.
example: Archiving 400M historical activity records to a Big Object keeps them queryable by the defined index while removing them from the transactional data model.

means: Queries filtering on non-indexed fields on large objects hit a row-count threshold and are killed. Indexed, selective filters are the difference between working and timing out.
example: A query on a 6M-record object filtering by a non-indexed text field throws a non-selective query exception. Filtering on an indexed field returns instantly.
